item.title: Palau Visitors Authority reports 76% tourism recovery from pre-pandemic levels
item.description: Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels. There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.
item.content:encoded:
Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels.

There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.

As of September, 63,948 people had traveled to Palau, meaning the country is on track to exceed last year’s total arrivals.

The Visitors Authority says that in 2025, Palau recorded the highest number of American, Australian and European tourists in the nation’s history. China remained Palau’s top visitor source market, with Taiwan ranking second.

The average visitor stay in Palau was a record 5.9 nights in 2025.

item.title: PBS Guam to host annual pledge drive Saturday
item.description: PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday. The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.
item.content:encoded:
PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday.

The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.

The annual fundraiser supports PBS Guam’s educational, cultural, and locally produced programming. The station relies on contributions from viewers, government, and foundations to continue providing educational content and sharing Guam’s stories.

PBS Guam is offering pledge gifts based on donation amounts. Donors who contribute $75 will receive a PBS Guam merchandise mystery box. A $100 donation includes a windbreaker, tote bag, director’s hat, and one year of PBS Passport access. A $150 donation includes all four gifts and one year of PBS Passport access, which provides an on-demand library of PBS programs, shows, and documentaries.

The pledge drive will air on KGTF Channel 12 and stream through the PBS App and YouTube at youtube.com/pbsguam . Rebroadcasts will air on KGTF Channel 12 every Sunday evening throughout Nov.

Community members can donate online at pbsguam.org/support or call 671-734-5483 for more information.

item.title: Regulators greenlight landmark solar project for CNMI
item.description: After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers. The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth
item.content:encoded:
After weeks of public hearings, scrutiny and debate, CNMI regulators on Thursday approved a landmark solar power project that officials say could reduce the commonwealth's dependence on imported fuel and bring long-term savings to utility customers.

The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission voted unanimously to approve the power purchase agreement and related contracts between the Commonwealth Utilities Corp. and developer Eastern Power Solutions, clearing a major hurdle for the proposed $500 million renewable energy initiative.

The project would establish a utility-scale solar and battery energy storage system for CUC and has drawn significant public attention amid concerns over its costs, financing structure and long-term impact on ratepayers.

The vote came just two days before an Oct. 31 deadline set by Eastern Power Solutions, which previously warned regulators it would withdraw its proposal if a decision was not reached. The company said the deadline was tied to financing requirements and a Dec. 31, 2027, federal tax-credit deadline critical to the project's economic viability.

Acting Chair Bruce Camacho and Commissioner Jack Angelo voted in person, while Commissioner James Mendiola participated virtually from Tinian.

"We've had a great turnout. We've had a lot of great public input," Mendiola said before the vote. He said commissioners had spent countless hours reviewing the extensive legal and financial documentation supporting the project.

"There are no easy decisions for the CNMI," Mendiola said. "There's an element of risk on both sides, and we have to weigh the risk."

Camacho said commissioners thoroughly reviewed the proposal despite concerns raised in public testimony and written comments.

"I think we've done everything on our side to properly review this proposal," he said.

Angelo rejected suggestions that the commission was responsible for delays, noting regulators identified issues involving land documentation and liability protections that required correction before approval.

"Our goal was to protect the ratepayers, but also regulate and oversee the utilities," Angelo said.

CPUC legal counsel James Sirok said concerns raised during the review process were adequately addressed and that nothing remained that should prevent commissioners from voting on the proposal.

Following the vote, CUC Executive Director Kevin Watson said the project represents a significant step toward modernizing the commonwealth's power system.

"We're on the way to making improvements within the utilities and CNMI, and these improvements will help our customers bring us forward with renewable power," Watson told reporters.

Watson said electricity generated under the agreement is expected to cost about 18.5 cents per kilowatt-hour for 25 years without escalation, compared with roughly 44 cents per kilowatt-hour today.

While immediate savings are not expected, Watson said lower fuel costs could begin benefiting customers once construction is completed and the solar facilities begin generating power, likely in 2028.

The primary solar facility is planned for the Naftan area near Saipan International Airport. Watson said CUC hopes to break ground soon and celebrate the project's launch with the community in the coming weeks.

item.title: Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate
item.description: Updated October 30, 2026 at 9:28 AM ChST Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race , which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 30, 2026 at 9:28 AM ChST

Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race , which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.

That story detailed efforts by Democratic campaign operatives to recruit what Republicans have long alleged is a spoiler candidate whose presence on the ballot could confuse voters and siphon support from the GOP incumbent. The two candidates share the name Dan Sullivan.

NPR hasn't independently confirmed the Times ' reporting, but it's roiled the Senate race just days before Election Day. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is hoping to flip the seat for her party.

The Times ' story is based on interviews and communications among Peltola's attorneys and advisers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Democrats have long denied involvement in the non-incumbent Sullivan's candidacy, and both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC reiterated those denials after the Times story published.

While campaigning Wednesday, Peltola called the story a distraction, according to Alaska Public Media , and the non-incumbent Sullivan did not respond to Alaska Public Media's requests for comment. He has previously said it was his decision to run for Senate.

"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan, said in a statement . President Trump called it "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level," in an online post .

Trump's Justice Department had already sought to intervene in the Senate race , asking a court last week to delay certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a small margin. The legal effort cited potential voter confusion stemming from the second Sullivan on the ballot.

Election law experts had broadly criticized the DOJ's case as weak , in part because the Constitution grants states control over elections.

The Sullivan candidacies had already been probed by state officials, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the non-incumbent Sullivan could appear on the general election ballot.

Justice Department officials said Thursday the Times ' story expands its options for investigating the Senate race, and it filed an amended complaint citing the new reporting.

And in the wake of the Times story, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said Wednesday night that he is directing the state's Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

It's unclear what laws could have been violated.

Trickery has been fairly common in politics, and it can be difficult to write laws that prevent shenanigans, according to Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who's co-authored a book on dirty tricks in campaigns.

"There's just a lot of tricks," Kamarck told NPR. "There's old ones. There's new ones. In this day and age, the internet makes it really easy to get the word out, both on a trick or, frankly, on a correction to a trick. But it's pretty standard fare for campaigns."

At times major-party advisers will seek to boost third-party candidates, in an effort to undercut the other major-party's candidate. Some voters who spoke with Alaska Public Media compared the new reporting about the Sullivan case to Republican groups' spending in support of a Democrat who's a federal prisoner in New York but who's on Alaska's U.S. House ballot .

The second, non-incumbent Sullivan advanced to the general election after Alaska's nonpartisan primary that sends the top four vote-getters to the fall ballot.

Alaska Public Media found mixed reactions to the Times ' reporting , with some residents frustrated that it's drawing attention from other issues, and others expressing skepticism that voters would be confused. The ballot notes which Sullivan is the Republican incumbent.

Some experts have pointed out that all the news about the second Sullivan's candidacy could reduce any voter confusion. And because the state has a ranked-choice voting system for the general election, if voters are confused, they could rank both Sullivans and not rank Peltola.

Whether voters want to keep the state's unique election system is also on the general election ballot .

NPR's Hansi Lo Wang and Ryan Lucas contributed reporting.

item.content:encoded:
Sir Patrick Stewart's most famous characters tackled concepts such as honor, morality and courage. He played Professor X in the X-Men franchise and Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the starship USS Enterprise, on the show St ar Trek: The Next Generation and its later spinoff, Picard .

Stewart died Wednesday at 86. A post on his Facebook and Instagram pages said he died at home in Los Angeles after a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."

Although he was beloved for playing compassionate father figures who united families of misfits, Stewart's own upbringing in Yorkshire, England, was harsh. He remembered his father as alcoholic and abusive. He found solace in school and, eventually, in Shakespeare. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and debuted on Broadway in 1970 in A Midsummer Night's Dream .

"To stand in the middle of an empty stage in an empty theater and feel that I was at home was everything," he told NPR in 2023 . "But it took a while for me to get there."

Stewart played alongside some of the best Shakespeareans of his time, including Judi Dench and Ian McKellen. He was lecturing on Shakespeare at UCLA when his name came up for the lead in a new series of Star Trek .

"Don't do this, Patrick," he remembered McKellen advising him. "You're a very good stage actor. That's where you ought to be. Don't do it."

But Stewart's agent had reassured him that the show was unlikely to make it past the first season. As the actor recalled to NPR, he was encouraged to take what he believed to be a quick and easy job. "'Do six months' work. Make some money for the first time in your life and get well known. Get a suntan, and go home.' And I thought, 'Yeah, that doesn't sound too bad. I could live with that.'"

But Star Trek: The Next Generation was a tremendous hit. It aired for seven seasons, from 1987 to 1994. Stewart was embraced by fans, who adored the character's penchant for Earl Grey tea and cool-headed leadership, with such signature phrases as "Engage!" and "Make it so!"

But success on the starship Enterprise came at a cost. Throughout his career, Stewart portrayed only a handful of Shakespeare's leading men. He put some of that character energy into an award-winning, one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol , in which Stewart played more than 40 roles.

By the beginning of the 21st century, Stewart had reestablished himself on stage while also lending his voice to numerous big-budget animated films. He went on to dominate another blockbuster franchise, the X-Men, beginning in 2000. He'll appear for the last time in his role as Professor Charles Xavier in the upcoming movie Avengers: Doomsday .

As for his signature role, Stewart thought he was done playing Picard. But a team of producers — including writer Michael Chabon — had different ideas. They pitched him a new show, Star Trek: Picard , that began streaming on the CBS service now called Paramount+ in 2020.

"I would've been happy just shaking Patrick Stewart's hand and telling him how much I loved him on Star Trek ," Chabon told NPR . "But to be able to actually write words that he will speak and act is — it's incredible."

In the show, Picard is struggling with the psychological damage that led to leaving Starfleet. The performance is vintage Stewart. His character is keen-eyed, haunted, weary, yet joyful. While this Picard was trapped in the past, Patrick Stewart spent his career charting the future.

item.title: Lost your spark? The "silent sister" of depression, and a quiz to spot her
item.description: Some people with clinical depression can't get out of bed. But what about those who exhibit other signs of depression who never stop moving, and may double down on their work? Psychiatrist Dr. Judith Joseph says the second group often goes unnoticed, even by the people living it. She calls it "high-functioning depression": people who keep meeting their obligations at work and at home while quietly
item.content:encoded:
Some people with clinical depression can't get out of bed. But what about those who exhibit other signs of depression who never stop moving, and may double down on their work?

Psychiatrist Dr. Judith Joseph says the second group often goes unnoticed, even by the people living it. She calls it "high-functioning depression": people who keep meeting their obligations at work and at home while quietly losing the ability to feel pleasure.

"When you are joyful, you have better physical health, you have better relationships, you have better productivity at work," Joseph said in an interview for the Your Turn podcast . "So why don't we prioritize it?"

At the center of Joseph's work is anhedonia: a reduced ability to feel joy, pleasure or interest in things that once brought those feelings. Joseph describes it as "the silent sister" of depression.

"One sister is depressed, and crying, and not getting out of bed, and getting all the attention," she says. "The other one is quiet and numb." Anhedonia may not seem like a crisis in the classic sense, Joseph says. "But it is an existential crisis, and it's not something to ignore."

In a peer-reviewed study published in the journal Cureus, Joseph and colleagues interviewed adults using a set of questionnaires designed to assess high-functioning depression, trauma and anhedonia.

The results supported the researchers' hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Participants with higher anhedonia scores also had higher high-functioning depression scores.

Parents and caregivers had the highest anhedonia and high-functioning depression scores in the study.

The authors note that high-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5, the manual clinicians use to diagnose mental health conditions. They say that is part of the problem: people who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they reach burnout.

Joseph says she often sees the pattern in women who are the steady presence for everyone around them. They are so focused on their responsibilities at work and at home that they don't realize they are burned out, or close to it.

"But eventually something's gonna give," she said. "Either they do break down and they have a clinical depression and they lose their functioning, they go into distress or crisis, or they physically break down."

She said she has seen patients end up in the emergency room without understanding why, only to learn they had been carrying unresolved emotional pain.

Joseph said the pattern is common in professions that discourage vulnerability, including her own. In medicine, she said, crying after a patient died was seen as weakness.

"In medicine, we focus on the crisis," Joseph said. "You're [taught] to look for the mania, for the psychosis." She believes there should be more focus on anhedonia, the loss of sense of joy.

Joseph developed an anhedonia quiz based on the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale, a measure of the capacity to feel pleasure that was published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

The questionnaire asks about everyday experiences, such as whether you have trouble enjoying praise, whether you savor your meals or other small pleasures, and whether you struggle to enjoy your work or accomplishments because they never feel good enough.

The quiz is not a diagnostic tool. It's an invitation to take stock of what might be standing in the way of a fuller, more joyful life. If you'd like to take the quiz, you'll be asked to share your email to see the results.

In her book, "High Functioning: Overcome Your Hidden Depression and Reclaim Your Joy," Joseph also outlines a framework she calls the Five V's:

Joseph says anhedonia appears across many conditions, in many people in midlife and other times, too. "It's something that we need to learn how to detect," she said, because it can be a silent problem.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988, to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Want to know more? Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.content:encoded:
New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.

A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.

Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.

Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.

For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.

Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.

Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?

To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.

He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.

"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.

In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.

That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.

"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.

Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.

"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.
